title: Lukewarm (Apocalypse 3:14–22)
tomorrow: I stand at the gate and knock

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephesus: busy, faithful, and missing its first love. Your line was the first charity.

You order a coffee and take a sip. Not hot. You'd have happily taken iced coffee, cold and sharp, or a steaming cup that warms your hands. But this one has sat under the lamp too long, and it's neither. You set it down and don't pick it up again. Everyone knows the face people make at a lukewarm drink. The last of the seven letters in the Apocalypse uses that face, and it goes to a city that had money, comfort and, if the historians are right, a water problem.
screen: `A COFFEE, NEITHER HOT NOR COLD.` → `THE FACE EVERYONE MAKES.` → `THE LETTER TO LAODICEA.`

segments.voice: Laodicea was rich, a banking town known for fine wool and for an eye medicine. The Roman historian Tacitus records that when an earthquake struck it in the year sixty, the city rebuilt from its own wealth, without help from Rome. Now Christ's words to its church, in the Douay-Rheims: "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold, nor hot. I would thou wert cold, or hot. But because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold, nor hot, I will begin to vomit thee out of my mouth." Strong language: the face at the coffee cup. Many scholars point to the city's water. Nearby Hierapolis had famous hot springs, good for healing. Colossae, not far off, had cold, fresh water, good for drinking. Laodicea's water, on this reading, came through a long aqueduct and arrived tepid. Read that way, hot and cold aren't zealous and hostile. Both are useful: one heals, one refreshes. Lukewarm does neither. And the church's problem matches the city's pride. Thou sayest, I am rich and have need of nothing, the letter goes on, and knowest not that thou art poor, and blind, and naked. A city of eye medicine, but blind. A city of wool, but naked. So Christ counsels them to get true gold, white garments and salve for their eyes from him. Then, so the harshness isn't misread: "Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise." A rebuke from someone who wants them back, not a door slammed. The very next verse is about a door, and who is standing outside it.
screen: `A RICH CITY THAT REBUILT ITSELF.` · `NEITHER COLD NOR HOT.` · `HOT HEALS, COLD REFRESHES.` · `RICH, BUT POOR, BLIND AND NAKED.` · then, large: `SUCH AS I LOVE, I REBUKE.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing today you'd normally do half-there: the dishes, a walk, a talk with a child, a prayer, a piece of work. Picture doing it with all of you, phone away, no rushing toward the next thing; not more effort, just more presence. If you pray, offer that one thing to God, done warmly; if not, simply commit to it in your mind.
Lukewarm. Apocalypse three: neither cold nor hot, neither refreshing nor healing, comfortable and half-there. Today's word.
Your line: not lukewarm. Hot heals, cold refreshes, and both are worth something. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 622 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: I STAND AT THE GATE AND KNOCK.`

howItsDone: Catholic spiritual writers have long warned against lukewarmness, or spiritual sloth, and Catholics often fight it with small, regular commitments: a daily prayer time, weekly Mass, a monthly confession, done wholeheartedly.

original.note: Greek: lukewarm, tepid (Apocalypse 3:16), the only time the word appears in the New Testament.

trapdoor: what you thought: lukewarm means not religious enough.
what it means: comfortable, self-satisfied, half-there: neither healing like hot water nor refreshing like cold.
what a scholar hears: Laodicea's tepid aqueduct water, between Hierapolis's hot springs and Colossae's cold water; and Tacitus on its self-funded rebuilding.

chat.says: Why would Jesus rather someone be cold than lukewarm? Isn't cold worse?
options: On one reading, hot water heals and cold refreshes; lukewarm does neither.
Because Laodicea was too poor to care, and he wanted them to work harder.
Because cold means quiet faith, and he wanted them to stop showing off.
chat.meaning: Many scholars read it by the water: Hierapolis's hot springs healed, Colossae's cold water refreshed. Lukewarm Laodicea did neither, and Christ rebukes because he loves.

notes: Laodicea's banking, black wool and 'Phrygian powder' eye medicine: commonly cited background (Strabo, Galen). Confirm.
Tacitus, Annals 14.27: Laodicea recovered from an earthquake (AD 60) by its own resources without Roman aid. Confirm the year.
Water reading (hot Hierapolis, cold Colossae, tepid aqueduct water at Laodicea): a widely held scholarly reading (Rudwick and Green, 1958), framed as 'many scholars point to'. Confirm.

The tepid-aqueduct reading is itself debated (some argue the water was not notably tepid, or that the image is simply about usefulness); the script now says 'on this reading'. The eye-medicine link also rests on later sources (Galen). Confirm framing.
3:17–18 paraphrased in near-Douay wording without quotation marks.
χλιαρός as a New Testament hapax: confirm.
Note: in the book's order Laodicea is the seventh and last of the letters; the hook calls it 'the last of the seven letters'.
